results.title: Brown Spots on Tomato Leaves? Could Be Early Blight - Here's How I Fixed It
results.description:
Brown spots on your tomato leaves could mean early blight — a fairly common tomato diseases in the home garden. The good news? If you catch it early, it's very treatable without reaching for anything synthetic.

In this video, I walk through exactly how to identify Alternaria solani (early blight) on tomatoes, trace how it likely got there, and run through the three-part organic pest control treatment I used in my own garden: pruning infected tissue, opening up the air gap under the canopy, and finishing with a biofungicide application using Revitalize — a biology-based fungus treatment that works with your soil, not against it.

If your tomato plants are showing yellowing lower leaves or dark, concentric target spots, this video will help you figure out what you're looking at — and what to do about it.

results.title: 💚 The #1 Reason Your Plant's Leaves Are Turning Brown & Crispy 🍂
results.description:
Are the edges of your beautiful houseplant leaves turning brown, dry, and crispy? It is one of the most frustrating and common problems for plant parents! While it might look like your plant is dying, brown tips are actually your plant's way of trying to communicate with you. In this video, we play "plant detective" and break down the top reasons why your leaves are getting crispy, and exactly how to stop it from happening to new growth!

📖 Read our full, in-depth troubleshooting guide on Brown, Crispy Edges here: 
👉 https://houseplant101.com/problems/brown-crispy-edges/


💡 Brown & Crispy Edges Quick Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet:

💧 Underwatering: This is the most common culprit! If the soil is completely bone dry and the lower leaves are crisping up and falling off, your plant is incredibly thirsty. Give it a deep, thorough soak!

💦 Low Humidity: Tropical plants (like Ferns, Calatheas, and Monsteras) are used to jungle moisture. If the air in your home is too dry, especially in the winter with the heater running, the edges of their broad leaves will quickly crisp up.

🚰 Water Quality (Tap Water): Some plants (like Spider Plants, Dracaenas, and Calatheas) are highly sensitive to the fluoride, chlorine, and minerals found in standard tap water. These chemicals build up in the leaf tips and burn them! Switch to filtered, distilled, or rainwater.

🧂 Fertilizer Burn: Did you recently fertilize? Too much plant food can cause a buildup of salts in the soil, which burns the roots and leads to crispy leaf edges. Always dilute your fertilizer!

✂️ Can You Cut the Brown Off? Yes! The brown parts are dead and will never turn green again. You can use sterilized scissors to trim away the crispy edges—just be sure to leave a tiny sliver of brown so you don't cut into the healthy green tissue and cause further damage.

Dark spots with yellow halo          → Fungal infection
Tiny pale dots, stippling pattern    → Spider mites
Soft translucent mushy patches       → Cold damage
White powdery coating                → Powdery mildew
Silvery or bronze sheen              → Thrips damage
Pale bleached washed-out leaves      → Too much direct light
Dark almost black green leaves       → Not enough light
Wilting despite wet soil             → Root rot or root failure
Sticky coating on leaves             → Pest honeydew — check for aphids or scale
Leaves dropping while still green    → Environmental stress adjustment
Variegation reverting to solid green → Low light — remove all-green shoots
